control.text:
it has a mandate to collect all materials created by men as well as women (including diaries, correspondence, and personal collections). According to LIS staff, there is no one method of classifying the materials, but it is suggested that the materials be considered "a part of the broader literature of the world." However, the policy does not specifically ban materials of any gender or sexuality. The policy states that "All libraries should be aware of the possibility of a gender bias" in how books are assigned. LIS policy states:

In the interest of fairness to both men and women, the Librarian's Office and the LIS Archival Program (APS) will ensure that when we consider material created by women, men should not receive any extra consideration compared with women, even if the same work is also submitted in the name of a man.

However, "The Archival Program [APS] is not responsible for assigning a particular treatment of a work to the work submitted under a given individual's name," according to NOC guidelines. Further:

In the APS' view, to consider books submitted under the name of a woman "more carefully than books submitted under the name of a man is consistent with the APS' desire to encourage gender and other diversity in library collections. For this reason, we will be looking to make sure that the work submitted is equally worthy." For this reason, the APs will also be following the guidelines outlined above concerning "how an individual has been represented in any particular volume [of an author's work]."

The Library also has two gender studies centers:

Feminist Theory Centre

Feminist Theory Centre is a centre for feminist and queer studies at the University of Toronto. It provides a space for feminists to gather and engage with one another and with the broader public in conversations about, and analysis of, feminist and social movements and ideologies. For more information please visit:

A Feminist Studies Centre: Gender, Race, and Colonialism at the University of Toronto , by Laura Smith, Feminist Studies Centre, University of Toronto, 2002.

Women in Revolutionary Thought, by Angela Davis, Feminist Studies Centre, University of Toronto, 2002.

It is unclear what will happen to the proposed exhibit, if anything. But a representative of the museum was still working on Monday to find a way to get the display into the show.

"We are working on the idea," said museum director Barbara Burdge.

She declined to comment further on the exhibit, which was supposed to show up in October, even though the museum had been on course to present it that month.

"It can be a long process when the museum is first getting started," she said.
 the proposed exhibit.

But at least one organization is already planning a protest when it opens its doors on May 3. The city's Black Lives Matter group plans to distribute fliers and posters around the museum's doors on Monday.

"The Black Lives Matter group plans to protest the controversial exhibit, featuring a picture of the city's new police chief," reported the St. Louis Post-Dispatch in an item about its planned action. "Activists will display an official resolution from the Black Lives Matter activist group asking the museum to remove the exhibit."

Activists and others have asked the museum to do just that. "While we welcome anyone who is interested in examining police violence (including) African-American victims like Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown, Eric Garner and Tamir Rice, to the museum, any efforts to promote violence are inappropriate, divisive and counterproductive," said an online petition circulated in advance of the planned demonstration.

The original exhibit had to be scrapped when a police officer was shot dead in St. Louis a few weeks ago, prompting concern for the safety of visitors at the museum.

"We would love to have it back, but in light of the recent deaths of black men and black women — we just didn't have the time," Burdge said. "We're working on it and hopefully there's a solution in the next month or so.

There has been one positive result. The museum has already been visited by a growing number of protesters who say the planned exhibit — which will feature images of Ferguson on display — will give them a wrong impression about the police department there.

"The museum is not just a place, but a reflection of the communities we serve," said St. Louis Police Captain Ron Johnson, in an interview with the Post-Dispatch. "It is important that when you come and visit the museum, that you see the beauty of St. Louis in all its splendor. … If we can highlight these aspects to the diversity and positive, and highlight the negative as well, well, I think it can help to change some of the misconceptions and negative perceptions that people have."
